record.original_question: For three-dimensional isotropic composites made from two isotropic phases, are all effective conductivity functions sigma*(sigma) realizable by multiple-rank laminate microstructures? If the answer is yes, is it enough to use laminate constructions in which each lamination step is taken only along mutually orthogonal directions?

evidence.quote: Problem 4: For three-dimensional isotropic composites of two isotropic phases, are all possible conductivity functions σ∗(σ) achievable by multiple rank laminate microstructures and, if so, does it suffice to consider laminate microstructures where one laminates only in mutually orthogonal directions?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider three-dimensional periodic (or stochastically homogeneous) two-phase composites built from two isotropic linear conductors with scalar conductivities σ₁, σ₂ > 0, occupying volume fractions f and 1−f. For such a composite, the effective (homogenized) conductivity tensor σ* is defined via the standard cell problem for the steady-state conductivity equation ∇·(σ(x)∇u) = 0, and the composite is called isotropic when σ* = σ*·I is a scalar multiple of the identity. Let G(σ₁, σ₂) denote the set ("G-closure") of all pairs (f, σ*) realizable as f ranges over [0,1] and over all microgeometries producing an isotropic effective tensor.

A rank-N laminate is constructed inductively: a rank-1 laminate is a simple layering of the two phases (or of previously constructed laminates) along a single unit direction n₁; a rank-k laminate is obtained by laminating a rank-(k−1) laminate together with one of the pure phases (or another laminate) along a direction n_k, with separation of length scales between successive lamination steps. The laminate is called orthogonal if all lamination directions n_1, …, n_N are mutually orthogonal (so at most three distinct directions are used in three dimensions).

Question: 
(a) Is every isotropic effective conductivity σ* attainable by a two-phase isotropic 3D composite—i.e., every point of G(σ₁, σ₂)—realizable as the effective conductivity of some finite-rank laminate microstructure built from the two phases?
(b) If yes, does it suffice to restrict to orthogonal laminate microstructures, in which all lamination directions are mutually orthogonal?
artifact.category_tag: Homogenization and G-closure of conductivity composites
artifact.status_search_result: No source was found establishing the full G-closure of 3D two-phase isotropic conductivity composites by (orthogonal) finite-rank laminates. While many extremal points of the G-closure are known to be attainable by multi-rank laminates (Milton, Lurie–Cherkaev, Tartar, etc.), the general realizability question and the sufficiency of mutually orthogonal lamination directions in three dimensions appear to remain unresolved in the literature.

status_evidence.title: Bounds for effective properties of multimaterial two-dimensional conducting composites
status_evidence.snippet: Optimal structures are laminates of finite rank... bounds are known not to be optimal for all choices of parameters
status_evidence.claim: Even in 2D, the realizability of the full G-closure by laminates is subtle and only partially resolved; analogous 3D questions remain open.

status_evidence.title: Multiphase laminates of extremal effective conductivity in two dimensions
status_evidence.snippet: The first type of isotropic, multi-material structures proved optimal for the translation bound were described by Milton (1981).
status_evidence.claim: Laminate realizability of extremal isotropic effective conductivities is established only in special cases, supporting that the general 3D problem is open.
